rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer:
You need 53 blocks, with 16 active threads in the final block. The arithmetic is 10,000 = 52 × 192 + 16, so you round up to 53 blocks, launching 53 × 192 = 10,176 threads.
Interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check”: all 10,176 launched threads should check their index, and 176 are out of bounds and must skip processing.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after another. Each reads a consistent snapshot, and write-conflict checks generally prevent concurrent updates to the same row—not conflicting decisions based on reads.

For example, two doctors are on call, and at least one must remain. Both transactions read that both doctors are on call, then each switches a different doctor off call. Because they write different rows, both can commit, leaving nobody on call: that is write skew.

Atomicity ensures each transaction happens entirely or not at all; it does not protect this cross-row invariant. Serializable isolation, or correctly coordinated locking on a shared record, can prevent it.

review.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions equivalent to running one after another.
